Coping with Cravings
P
Phoenix123
Level 5 · Flourish · 2 days ago
Hey everyone — wanted to start a thread on cravings since I feel like we don't always talk openly about the day-to-day reality of it. For me, evenings are the hardest. After dinner when everything gets quiet, my brain just starts pulling. Anyone else have a time of day that's consistently harder?
K
KindredSpirit
Level 3 · Root · 2 days ago
Evenings too, but also when I drive past my old neighborhood. It's like my body remembers before my brain even registers what's happening. I've been doing the urge surfing exercise in the app — riding it out instead of fighting it. It doesn't make the craving disappear but it makes it feel survivable.
R
RisingTide
Level 4 · Bloom · 1 day ago
Work stress is my biggest trigger. I've started doing a 5-minute check-in with Sage before meetings I know are going to be rough. It's not magic but it takes the edge off enough that I can stay present. The key for me was catching it early — once I'm already in the thick of a craving it's so much harder to pull back.
N
NewDawn44
Level 3 · Root · 1 day ago
I didn't realize how much my cravings were tied to loneliness until I looked at 3 weeks of patterns data. It was so clear once I saw it laid out — strong cravings almost every weekend when I had nothing planned. Now I try to schedule something on Sundays just to have a reason to show up somewhere.
ME
VictoryWarrior (you)
Level 4 · Bloom · 22 hours ago
The Patterns feature was a turning point for me too @NewDawn44. I noticed my cravings spike after bad nights of sleep. Now I treat poor sleep as an early warning — I'll call my sponsor the next morning before things get hard rather than waiting until I'm already struggling.
P
Phoenix123
Level 5 · Flourish · 18 hours ago
That's such a good reframe @VictoryWarrior — treating warning signs as a cue to reach out proactively. I've been using the SOS tool a few times too. Just having something structured to focus on in that moment helps break the loop. The breathing exercise especially — I was skeptical but it genuinely works.
K
KindredSpirit
Level 3 · Root · 14 hours ago
Proud of everyone in this thread for talking about this openly. A craving doesn't mean you're weak or that something is wrong with you — it just means your brain is still healing. The craving is not the same as using.
R
RisingTide
Level 4 · Bloom · 6 hours ago
This community is honestly one of the things keeping me going. You all understand this in a way that's hard to explain to people outside of it. 52 days and counting.
N
NewDawn44
Level 3 · Root · 2 hours ago
52 days is incredible @RisingTide — we're all cheering for you. And for anyone reading this on a hard day: a craving is not a failure. It's just brain chemistry. You don't have to act on it. You can just let it pass. We're here.
ME

Connect · Recovery Support
Stress Management
R
RisingTide
Level 4 · Bloom · 1 day ago
Wanted to open a thread on stress because it's my single biggest trigger — more than any place or person. Work pressure especially. Has anyone found things that actually work? Not just in the moment but building a lower baseline over time?
P
Phoenix123
Level 5 · Flourish · 1 day ago
Exercise has been the most consistent thing for me. Even a 20-minute walk when I'm wound up makes a real difference. My nervous system needs somewhere to put the stress, or it just turns into craving. I don't think I fully understood how physical stress is until recovery.
K
KindredSpirit
Level 3 · Root · 22 hours ago
I've started doing the breathing exercises in the app before I even feel stressed — like a daily preventive thing rather than waiting for a crisis. It's made my baseline lower somehow. The 4-7-8 breath especially. Two minutes in the car before I walk into anything difficult.
N
NewDawn44
Level 3 · Root · 18 hours ago
Therapy has been the biggest thing for me. Understanding where my stress response comes from — a lot of it goes back much further than I realized — has made it less automatic. I still get stressed but I don't get hijacked by it as often. It took about 3 months before I noticed the difference.
ME
VictoryWarrior (you)
Level 4 · Bloom · 14 hours ago
I journal. I know it sounds small but getting the stress out of my head and onto paper breaks the loop. I started doing it right after dinner — which is when cravings tend to hit for me anyway — and it helps with both things at once. 10 minutes, no rules about what to write.
R
RisingTide
Level 4 · Bloom · 10 hours ago
That's a great idea about timing it intentionally @VictoryWarrior. I've been trying to build these practices into a routine rather than reaching for them in crisis mode. The Sage check-in feature is good for that — 5 minutes before something I know will be hard.
P
Phoenix123
Level 5 · Flourish · 5 hours ago
One thing I wish someone told me earlier: stress doesn't have to be dramatic to be dangerous. It's the low-level constant stuff that's worn me down more than the big events. Paying attention to that daily baseline — not just the spikes — has been one of the most important things in my recovery.
ME
Share your experience...
Connect · Recovery Support
Family Struggles
N
NewDawn44
Level 3 · Root · 2 days ago
Wanted to open a space to talk about family stuff. I think it's one of the hardest parts of recovery that doesn't always get talked about openly. My family is supportive, but they're also scared. Every time I'm having a hard day I can see the worry in their faces — and it makes me feel like I can't be honest with them.
K
KindredSpirit
Level 3 · Root · 2 days ago
I feel that so much. My parents' fear sometimes comes out as control — checking in constantly, not trusting me to manage my own schedule. I know it comes from love but it's exhausting, and sometimes it actually makes things harder. I haven't figured out how to talk to them about it yet.
P
Phoenix123
Level 5 · Flourish · 1 day ago
Rebuilding trust is the long game and I had to make peace with the fact that I can't rush it. I caused real harm when I was using, and the people who love me carry that. The most useful thing my therapist said: I don't get to set the timeline for their healing. That was hard to hear but it helped.
R
RisingTide
Level 4 · Bloom · 1 day ago
That's a really grounding reframe @Phoenix123. I've also had to work on not letting family tension become a reason to isolate — that's when I'm most at risk. Now I try to tell someone on my care team when things are rocky at home before it builds up.
ME
VictoryWarrior (you)
Level 4 · Bloom · 20 hours ago
The hardest conversation I've had in recovery was asking my mom to stop bringing up the past every time she got scared. It took multiple tries and it's still not perfect. But things are genuinely better now. Sometimes you have to advocate for the relationship you need, not just accept the one you have.
N
NewDawn44
Level 3 · Root · 16 hours ago
Thank you for sharing that @VictoryWarrior. I think a lot of us are just trying to survive interactions with family rather than actively shaping them. That reframe — advocating for the relationship you need — is something I'm going to hold onto.
K
KindredSpirit
Level 3 · Root · 8 hours ago
For anyone whose family just doesn't understand and may never fully: it's okay to grieve that. You can love people and also accept their limits. Building community here and elsewhere isn't a consolation prize — it's part of what makes recovery sustainable when family can't carry all of it.
ME

Connect · Recovery Support
Managing Pain
R
RisingTide
Level 4 · Bloom · 2 days ago
Wanted to bring up something I haven't seen discussed much — chronic pain in recovery. I have a back injury from before I started using, and the pain is still real. It's complicated because pain was part of why I started in the first place. Is anyone else navigating this?
P
Phoenix123
Level 5 · Flourish · 2 days ago
Yes — lower back pain here too. My doctor and I had a careful conversation about non-opioid management. I'm on a combination of PT, a nerve block, and occasional NSAIDs. It's not perfect but it's manageable. Having a provider who actually understands addiction medicine made all the difference.
K
KindredSpirit
Level 3 · Root · 1 day ago
Heat, stretching, and — surprisingly — the mindfulness exercises in the app. I was skeptical that breathing could touch physical pain, but there's something real in changing your relationship to the sensation rather than just trying to eliminate it. Doesn't fix it, but makes it liveable.
N
NewDawn44
Level 3 · Root · 1 day ago
The hardest part for me is that pain spikes my cravings more than almost anything else. My brain has a very direct wire between 'hurt' and 'want relief.' What helps is naming that connection out loud — when pain flares I say 'this is a craving trigger' and it creates a little distance between the sensation and the urge.
ME
VictoryWarrior (you)
Level 4 · Bloom · 22 hours ago
Exercise has paradoxically helped my pain AND my cravings. I started swimming — low impact, and there's something about the rhythm of it that quiets everything down. It took about 6 weeks to feel any real difference, but now I notice when I've skipped it for a few days.
R
RisingTide
Level 4 · Bloom · 12 hours ago
For anyone dealing with this — please advocate hard for an addiction-aware provider. A lot of general practitioners don't know how to manage pain in people with OUD and will either undertreat out of fear or not understand the risks. You deserve good pain care and good addiction care. Both are possible.
P
Phoenix123
Level 5 · Flourish · 4 hours ago
Seconding this completely. The pain is real and it deserves real treatment. Recovery doesn't mean you have to suffer. It just means the treatment has to be thoughtful. Don't let anyone tell you otherwise.
ME
Share your experience...
Connect · Recovery Support
Making New Friends
K
KindredSpirit
Level 3 · Root · 3 days ago
This might sound basic but I genuinely don't know how to make friends anymore. My whole social world was tied up in using — the people, the places, all of it. I don't have a problem staying sober, but I'm lonely in a way I didn't expect and I'm not sure where to start.
N
NewDawn44
Level 3 · Root · 3 days ago
I felt this acutely around the 30-day mark. What helped was NA meetings — not just for the recovery support but because the people there are actually building sober lives and want to know each other. I've made two real friends from my home group. It took a few months of just showing up.
P
Phoenix123
Level 5 · Flourish · 2 days ago
Volunteering changed things for me. I started helping at a food bank on Saturday mornings and now I look forward to it every week. You're working alongside people toward a shared purpose — that's a natural foundation for connection. Nobody knows you're in recovery unless you tell them.
R
RisingTide
Level 4 · Bloom · 2 days ago
I was intentional about picking up a hobby that requires being around the same people regularly — I joined a recreational volleyball league. I'm not good at it, which is actually helpful because it gives everyone something to laugh about. Low stakes, same faces every week, natural reason to keep showing up.
ME
VictoryWarrior (you)
Level 4 · Bloom · 1 day ago
I've been honest with a few people I've gotten close to about being in recovery, and it's gone better than I feared. Not with everyone, and not right away — I've learned to feel out whether someone is safe before sharing. But the friendships where they actually know me are much deeper.
K
KindredSpirit
Level 3 · Root · 18 hours ago
These are all really helpful. I think I've been waiting to feel "ready" before putting myself out there — but maybe that feeling doesn't come first. You build connection by showing up before you feel ready.
N
NewDawn44
Level 3 · Root · 10 hours ago
That's exactly it. Recovery itself taught me that you act your way into a new way of thinking, not the other way around. Same thing with friendship. You show up, you're a little awkward, you come back. Eventually it becomes real.
P
Phoenix123
Level 5 · Flourish · 3 hours ago
Also — this community counts. I know it's an app and it might feel less 'real' than face-to-face. But the people in these threads are genuinely supporting each other through hard things. That's real friendship, even if it looks different.
ME
